title: Take the cost out of the router's refusals

blocks.text: The parcel router tries its routing rules in order, and the first rule that applies picks the hub. A rule that doesn't apply throws `NoRouteException`, and `route()` catches it and tries the next rule; a typical parcel is refused by forty rules before one applies. The router is the busiest service in the depot, and a profile of it shows 40% of its CPU time inside `NoRouteException`'s constructor. When no rule applies at all, the failure goes to the caller and into the error log, and the on-call engineer has to be able to see where it came from and which rule refused last.

items: `unroutable(...)`, the exception `route()` throws when no rule applies.

cases.says: the first rule that doesn't refuse picks the hub
a parcel no rule applies to reaches the caller as an exception naming the parcel
a rule's refusal captures no stack trace and still names the rule and the parcel
the failure that leaves route() is an ordinary exception with a stack trace, not the cheap refusal
the failure that leaves route() keeps the last refusal as its cause

origin.section: Filling In the Stack Trace Is Most of the Cost; Skip It Only Where Nobody Reads the Trace

concepts: An exception without a stack trace prints no at lines, so a failure that leaves the code is an ordinary exception with the miss as cause.

writableStackTrace = false (or an overridden fillInStackTrace) skips the stack walk that makes up most of an exception's cost, so it suits exceptions used as control flow that never leave the code that catches them.
